-does not have this aspect. If we say that we are going to take advantage of the fact that a certain number of people are going to gamble at all times, they are going to buy sweepstakes tickets, they are going to play bingo, there are many other more lucrative sources of revenue that we could probably consider. For instance, we could decide whether we are going to sell morphine, or legalize or license some of the oldest professions. There are many other vices in which people indulge. We know there are drug addicts, and we could just raise the price of drugs, for instance. Today the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss LaMarsh) reported to the house that we are trying to persuade young people not to smoke. Why do that? Why not just raise the price of cigarettes and get everybody to smoke? This is the real issue here.
Let us suppose that we decide gambling is not such a big vice, that we are all going to do it, so let us legalize it. We then change to some extent the morals involved in this question. This is what we are asked to do here. It will always be quasi moral, quasi legal, and this is the element that invites the unwelcome entrepreneur, whether we are talking about the whisky business or whatever it is. Some of my best friends are, or were, moonshiners. It was difficult for them to grasp the fact that the government or somebody else could make whisky and sell it but they could not. It no longer becomes a moral issue if we take this stand.
We are here dealing with future Canadians. I take it we would have a very respectable board or commission, composed of judges, professors, and so on regulating the bookie business. It is going to be very difficult to convince other people that they have no right to do this. They ask, if it is moral for the government to do it, why is it not moral for them to do it. This is the real issue. I do not know that I have made up my mind one way or the other. Whether the element of pure gambling is involved, it is still a moral question to this extent, that the number of people who will take advantage of sweepstakes will cause serious concern to this country, our economy and our way of living. But nevertheless this is the question the house must decide at this time; not that this will be an 28902-5-3264

isolated instance all on its own and there will be no other similar questions to decide, because we will still be asked to decide whether we are going to legalize bingo games or lotteries of all kinds, controlled or uncontrolled.
Therefore if the hon. member, instead of presenting this bill had presented a bill to the house to amend the Criminal Code, perhaps this would have been a better way to achieve his object, because if we are going to legalize gambling we should do it with proper regulation, in the proper way, through the Criminal Code, and all we would have to say would be, "Gambling is not such a bad thing after all. We have lived with it for centuries and we are going to go ahead with it". For these reasons I would ask this house not to support this bill.

Mr. Chairman, at the time of adjournment I was referring to the fact that we believe in one commission rather than ten; and we emphasize the necessity of there being two judges on such a commission. I had mentioned earlier the attitude taken by the Right Hon. W. L. Mackenzie King in that connection. Before I refer to what he said I might mention that as far back as 1903 the Conservative party took its stand in this regard and, as of the redistribution following the legislation of 1900, as a party we accepted the principle of a reference to a judicial tribunal with rules for the guidance of that tribunal. In that connection I refer to Hansard for 1903. It was also proposed that county boundaries should not be laid down as a principle except subject to certain conditions. It was proposed to refer the whole question to a judicial tribunal to be composed of chief justices of the supreme courts of the several provinces. The resolution in question read as follows, as reported at column 12376 of Hansard for September 25, 1903:
First, that a commission to consist of the chief justices of the highest courts of judicature in each of the provinces of Canada shall be appointed for the purpose of fixing the boundaries of each constituency entitled to elect a member or members of the House of Commons-
Then after some further general remarks the resolution continued:
-that such commission in so doing shall consider the distribution of population according to the then latest distribution of population according to the then latest census of Canada and the public interest and convenience, and shall particularly have regard so far as practicable to the boundaries of the counties, municipalities and cities.
MacGregor Dawson in his book says this:
Thus Mr. Mackenzie King in 1933 suggested a commission of six judges from different provinces (three to be nominated by the government, three by the opposition).
Furthermore, I recall very well Mr. King's speech in the House of Commons on July 15, 1947 when, as he often did, he quoted what he had said on other occasions. On this occasion he said, as reported on page 5648 of Hansard for that year:
My own view, and I have come to it after observing pretty carefully what has been taking place and what has been said in debate in this house as well as in the corridors, is that redistribution should be taken out of the hands of the House of Commons, where the parties are immediately interested, and should be put in the hands of a commission of judges. I would have that commission composed of judges selected in equal numbers by both sides of the house. The redistribution, if it is carried out in a fair way, has not to do with party advantage at all. It ought to have solely to do with seeking to effect a fair and impartial division of the constituencies.

And then he goes on to deal with the question in a general way.
On June 28, 1952-I am not going to follow Mr. King in this regard-I said on that occasion that I would set out in some detail the plans followed in this regard in other countries. I am sure with the reinforcement of Mr. King's views in this connection, and with the expressed desire of the Secretary of State to listen to the voice of reason, this is one matter which he will be willing to reconsider. Because if the plan be to appoint ten commissions across Canada, there will be as many different angles to the decisions arrived at. Regardless of whether there is one member representing the country as a whole, the same person being on each commission, there will be uncertainty and great difference of opinion.
Looking back to what has been done in other countries, South Africa has three superior court judges to consider the redistribution question. New Zealand has two commissions composed of five members on each, Australia, to which reference has been made, has one for each state consisting of the surveyor general, the chief electoral officer, with the chairman nominated by the governor general, who I think is really the governor in council. The United Kingdom has a chairman, the registrar general, the director general of the ordinance survey, and two other members.
I am not going to go into detail this evening because there will be every opportunity for that later, but I do want to point out some salient views which we hold in this regard. The first is that, to ensure that this would be an independent national commission, there should be one commission with a majority of judges on it. It is not for me to say what is in the bill, and I make no reference to it. But I point out that when in 1962 we introduced our measure there was no one more definite than the present Secretary of State in the view that under no circumstances should such a plan be accepted unless the names of those appointed were included in the bill. We took the stand that this had never been done previously. I am sure there has been no reconversion on the part of the Secretary of State, and in any appointments there should be I am confident that, in accordance with the spirit he has exhibited today in such abundant measure, he will see the wisdom of placing before us the names he has in mind.

If the right hon. gentleman would permit me, I should like to make one intervention. I know he does not want to misrepresent the position I took. I did take the position that I thought the names should be in the bill, or that the appointments
Redistribution Commission should be made by parliament. I still think that this should be done in some fashion. One thing I do want to make clear: I do not think it should be done by the governor in council.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR OFFICE OF REPRESENTATION COMMISSIONER AND READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION
speechtext:
I am clear about that; but whether it is done by the governor in council or otherwise, I am glad we have the certainty we now have that the hon. gentleman believes those names should be available to parliament in advance.
It is not for me to reveal what is in the bill but if, perchance, there were any provision whereby in the absence of agreement between the government and the opposition the governor in council would make the determination, I am sure the governor in council would be making quite a few of the appointments. That is something the hon. gentleman feels should be prepared against, so I am sure the government will be in a position, before the bills are in front of us, to indicate who in its opinion, should constitute this commission. There has been, as I said a moment ago, a large measure of agreement surrounding the person of the chief electoral officer, and I hope a similar measure of agreement can continue with respect to the other appointments to be made.
And now we come to one of the most difficult and complex problems facing us, a problem which has exercised the thinking of successive administrations in the past. From the very beginning of our country and throughout the years the principle has always been accepted that a rural seat should not be required to have the same population as an urban constituency. The reason for this is apparent to all who have represented rural constituencies. I was particularly struck by what the Secretary of State said today. Seasoned first in Manitoba, and then ripened in Newfoundland, he has an appreciation of the country as a whole which few possess. Travel widens, and experience of that kind always expands the scope of wisdom, and I am sure, Mr. Chairman, you would agree that this scope on the part of the hon. gentleman has been greatly increased since he took over Newfoundland. However, there has been a great deal of discussion on this subject. The same problem exists in the United States. As the house knows, there was a judgment of the supreme court of the United States in 1962 on the subject of constituencies-districts, as they are called in that country. In that judgment it was pointed out that throughout the years rural districts in the United States have had lower populations than have urban districts. It has been an acceptable situation, and the judgment places, as it were, the handwriting on the wall for the practice in this

Redistribution Commission regard. It has been a long, difficult and trying experience to determine what is fair and what is reasonable. A similar difficulty has been encountered in our provinces, as well. Without designating any one of them in particular, I can think of one province in which two cities have almost half of the population but only one quarter of the seats in the provincial legislature. It is difficult to arrive at a fair basis of representation.
Certainly, I would be the last to argue that there is the fairness there should be when one constituency may have a population of a quarter of a million and another a population of less than twenty thousand. I am not thinking now of the two northern constituencies which, as the hon. gentleman has said, have guaranteed representation, just as the provinces by the sea have guaranteed representation in the parliament of Canada. It is a difficult problem. There are some who suggest that under the present system Canadians are governed by a rural tyranny. I think it was McGeachy who, referring to those in the country, said: "The tyranny of the yokel will be hard to break". That was in an article which appeared in the Financial Post. It is not a very good basis upon which to proceed, but it is indicative of a state of mind.
We must endeavour to bring about, with reasonable regard for the urbanization that is taking place, a basis of representation which will not be unfair to those large rural areas which are so difficult to represent in parliament. It is not for me to place before the committee any of the temperate views expressed in the bill that is to be introduced, but I am going to place before the house what the view was of the members of the Conservative party when it formed the government of Canada. I know there was criticism that we should have proceeded earlier than we did with this matter. Until today that criticism was tenable, but after listening to the Secretary of State point out the length of period of time that will be necessary in order to bring about the change, full corroboration has now been given by him of the course which we followed.
I recognize fully the difficulties that are inherent in any decision that will be made. We worked on this matter at length. The Secretary of State has spoken of the interviews he has had with numbers of knowledgeable people on this question. We did the same. What formula could we arrive at that would be fair to all? I am going to place our views on record, and they represent our views today as they did when we introduced our bill in 1962.
We believe, as I said, that there should be one commission consisting of five members, one of whom shall be the person for the time

being holding the office of chief electoral officer of Canada and the remainder to be named in the proclamation. So we have that measure of agreement this evening between the government and the opposition, in that we agree that Mr. Castonguay is the type of person to occupy a position on this commission. Then we went on to deal with the ground rules, as it were. We said that the commission would have to make a report within a year and that in preparing its report the commission should be governed by certain rules. We said that the division of each province into electoral districts, and the description of the boundaries, should correspond as nearly as may be to the electoral quota of that province, that is to say, the quotient obtained by dividing the population of that province as ascertained by the census by the number of members of the House of Commons to be assigned to that province as calculated by the commission under section 11. There is no argument about that.
Then we mentioned the difficulty in connection with electoral districts represented by two members in the House of Commons. That is a problem, for example, in the city of Halifax. Throughout the years it has been a matter of tacit tradition and accepted policy in Halifax that one member shall belong to the Protestant faith and one member to the Roman Catholic faith. We have to make allowances for that.
What about representation by population? The old cry of "rep. by pop." almost caused people to resort to rebellion. It is a principle that must be accepted, subject to exceptions that are based on many considerations too numerous to outline at the moment. We also provided in our bill that attention should be given to special geographic considerations, including the sparsity or density of population of various regions of a province, the accessibility of such regions or the size or shape thereof, which appeared to the commission to render such a departure necessary or desirable. We think that is a consideration that should be placed in the statute as one of the ground rules.
We said that consideration should also be given by the commission to a departure from the principle of representation by population in the case of any special community or diversity of interests of the inhabitants which would render a departure necessary or desirable. That is pretty general in its terms but, as the minister said today, we must endeavour to allow for a reasonable degree of flexibility, so that the commission may exercise their responsibility in fairness and in justice.

We also provided for a departure wherever it appeared to the commission to be necessary or desirable, without causing excessive disparities of size between electoral districts, in order to take advantage of existing boundaries of counties, districts or other municipalities. One can think of old, traditional ridings in Quebec and Ontario which have been distinguished throughout the years for the representation they have had in the House of Commons. I have no plea to make for Prince Albert; and with a complete absence of bias and prejudice, of course, I point out that Prince Albert is the only constituency in Canada that has ever had three prime ministers. Sir Wilfrid Laurier, as Mr. Laurier, was elected in 1896. In those days when anyone accepted a position in the gift of the crown he immediately lost his constituency and following his elevation to the prime ministership he chose Quebec East.
Prince Albert also had Mr. Mackenzie King for many years. There is a constituency far removed from the centre of the nation which has contributed three of the fourteen prime ministers of this nation. Quebec East had Sir Wilfrid Laurier and the Right Hon. Louis St. Laurent. There are quite a number of other similar cases across Canada. Manitoba has been honoured twice by having prime ministers. Leaders of the opposition, too, have found kinship in a province far removed from their accustomed abode. All this indicates that every constituency, whether rural or urban, can make a contribution to the House of Commons.
We have the rule of "rep. by pop.", but whatever political scientists may say in this regard there must be a recognition of the fact, which I am sure is within the experience of all members representing rural ridings, that traditionally some degree of tolerance should be granted. My suggestion is that the commisison might depart from the electoral quota for the province in question, for any constituency, to the extent of not more than one third or less than one third. This means that if the quotient is 70,000 any constituency would be allowed to have no more than about 94,000 and no less than approximately 46,000. I place that before the committee as a fair and reasonable basis.
Now, I know that whatever we do will cause harm to some of our members. However, the attitude of good will in the house that was evinced in such an abundant measure this afternoon by the Secretary of State causes me to make the suggestion that this might be a reasonable basis. Someone will say, "That will have the effect of wiping out my constituency"-or someone else's constituency. But no matter what we do in order
Redistribution Commission to bring about a compromise, to bring about fairness and justice, there will be some who will suffer. Some might suggest 20 per cent.
I do not think that will cover the situation at all. I think that a 20 per cent tolerance would have very serious consequences. I do not think it is enough. I point out what the situation will be in the provinces of Ontario and Quebec, where ridings that have been represented through the years, which members have served with distinction, will find themselves obliterated if we follow the principle of representation by population literally.
It has been accepted in the United States that there must be a recognition of the fact that rural ridings will necessarily not have the same population as urban ridings, for many reasons that could be advanced and will be mentioned by other members. I suggest, therefore, that a one third tolerance will meet the situation. While it will not meet the position of many individual members in the house, it has in it the elements of fairness and justice. This is what we are trying to bring about.
The Secretary of State said that he hoped what we would do would be followed by other parliaments. I do not express the hope,
I express the certainty; because when we remove this cancer of political manipulation and operation on constituencies, without an anaesthetic, for political purposes we will have removed one of the most serious blights on the parliamentary system. Furthermore, I believe when this commission is of the opinion a direct application of the rules in any particular case is not practicable or would be likely to produce inequitable results, they may recommend a departure from the general rule.
There are many other matters with which I could deal, but other members will deal with them. I am trying to meet the problem without the rancour of experience, without going back once more to fan the embers of past controversies, but trying to deal with this subject in a fair and objective manner. The minister has stated that the house is going to have an opportunity to make a determination, that the government is prepared not to stand or fall on whatever bill may be produced but rather to ask for the counsel of the house. It is for this reason I have chosen to place these views before the committee. I hope that there will be a considerable amount of discussion of this proposal. This is not one of those things that can be rushed through. We are charting new courses. We are entering into an experiment. We are turning our backs on the past. All too often redistribution was an occasion for action to remove political adversaries. We are
5130	HOUSE OF
Redistribution Commission trying to end this, and for that reason I have set forth some of the general considerations we feel are necessary.
We feel that the appointment of ten commissions is not the answer to the problem. We feel that there should be a national commission. We feel that the representation on that commission, with the exception of he who holds the position of chief electoral officer or the position envisaged by the resolution, and possibly the surveyor general, should consist of judges who will be removed from politics and whose views will be accepted as a judicial decision based on the rules made by parliament. We feel that, in so far as the rural constituencies are concerned, there should be a tolerance of approximately one third.
Now, all of this will not place in the hands of the commission the power of a final decision. The decision must rest finally with parliament. We have to guard against setting up a commission that will be determining the rights of parliamentarians and, therefore, there must be final acceptance by parliament of whatever the recommendations of the commission may be. It is not for me to say what is in the bill that has been drafted. But generally speaking, I feel that we must assure that parliament shall finally determine the matter. I am not going to make any observations on what may be in the bill in that connection.
I believe I have covered what I set out to cover. If the same attitude is taken as was so evident today in the opening remarks of the Secretary of State, I am sure that we will evolve a plan that will be a credit to parliament, to our responsibility to assure the maintenance of the democratic process and, above all, that each of us will be acting in accordance with the dictates of justice rather than the compelling mandate of political consideration.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, both the Secretary of State and the Leader of the Opposition have had occasion in the course of their remarks to refer to the greatness of


our parliamentary institution. This is a sentiment to which we all subscribe. I believe all of us accept it as our responsibility to try and maintain that greatness, and indeed to do what we can to make this institution even greater for our having been here.
As one who has had the opportunity of participating in the parliamentary redistributions of the 'forties and the 'fifties, I sense already the possibility that this debate on redistribution may well be unique; it may well be unlike any other that we have had in our Canadian history. As I have indicated, I took part in two of these redistributions, those in each of the last two decades, and they were rather stormy, quite fiery and very contentious. I have also had occasion to read some of the earlier debates on redistribution, and I must say that by comparison the storms we had in the 'forties and 'fifties were games of tiddlywinks. As a matter of fact, it has not been in redistribution debates that parliament has proven its greatness. In the past these debates were occasions when hon. members exhibited proprietary interests in their own constituencies, in which one party tried to hurt the other, in which various injustices were done, and all told these debates have not been the brightest chapters of Canadian parliamentary history.
With that background I am delighted, as I am sure are all hon. members, that we are having the opportunity in this session of parliament to bring into being legislation that will remove the drawing of constituency boundaries from a parliamentary committee and put it in the hands of an independent commission. I had earlier planned on giving some details as to where parties stood on this matter in the past, but I confess that in view of the charms of Orpheus, otherwise known as the Secretary of State, and the endeavour of the Leader of the Opposition to match that charm, it is a bit difficult to remind Liberals and Conservatives of the details of their past on this question.

He did not like the redistribution that was being effected by the government in power at that time, so in 1933 he favoured an independent commission; but in 1943, when Mr. Coldwell asked if consideration was being given to redistribution by an independent commission, there was no answer, and likewise, the redistribution of that decade, which did not come until 1947, was put

through by a parliamentary committee on which the Liberals had a majority. Again in 1952 the same Liberals were in power and redistribution was done by a parliamentary committee rather than by an independent commission.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR OFFICE OF REPRESENTATION COMMISSIONER AND READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION
speechtext:
My hon. triend from Ville-neuve is interjecting. I happened to notice his name in one of these Hansard volumes, when he was here before as the hon. member for Pontiac, and I find that on one occasion he too voted against redistribution by an independent commission. I mention these things of the past just to indicate how pleased I am that we have reached this point of unanimity.
I was going to say that the Leader of the Opposition was quite correct in pointing out that the Conservative party, many years ago, started talking about redistribution by an independent commission, but somehow or another that talk was when it was in opposition. When it was in power, for example in the 'thirties, it did it the other way. Even in 1947, when I had the privilege of moving an amendment on second reading of a redistribution bill, that it be not now read a second time but that it be resolved that in the opinion of the house redistribution should be effected by an independent commission, only some 19 members of the Conservative party-mind you, they were the better ones -voted for that amendment. All the rest of them voted the other way.
So, there has been a slow process of education among the various parties. However, we have now reached the point where we all agree that no longer should redistribution be carried out by a parliamentary committee, no longer should we go through this kind of bitter experience in which hon. members try to protect their proprietary interests, as was the case in the nine or ten redistributions this country has had up to the present time.
Also, as the Leader of the Opposition has pointed out, his party when it was last in power did commit itself to the principle of redistribution by an independent commission. He has made it clear in what he said this evening that he may differ in some detail from the proposals to be made by the government, but at least the Conservative party, let it be said without qualification, committed itself while it was in power. I think this was the first time a government in power committed itself to redistribution by an independent commission. We now have the Liberals back in power, and for the first time 28902-5-327
Redistribution Commission in their experience as a party in power they have committed themselves to this same principle.
Mr. Chairman, this is good. We have now come to the point where we realize the seats we represent are not our personal possessions. We have come to the point where we realize that parliament belongs to the people of Canada and that we must find some way, other than doing it ourselves, to determine the boundaries of the constituencies that are represented in this house. I say again, this is good, and we may well have the opportunity in this debate to wipe out the memory of the nine or ten redistribution debates in the history of our country which make reading that does not add to the greatness of parliament.
I liked the suggestion of the Secretary of State that we might now put on our statute books a piece of legislation that would not make it necessary to make basic changes every ten years. The Leader of the Opposition echoed that, and turned that hope into confidence. I join with both of them in hope and confidence this will be the case, but it will be so only if we produce good legislation in this field at this time. I was glad to hear the Secretary of State make it clear that this is not a piece of legislation the details of which the government will make a matter of confidence, but rather that we start with the proposition that all of us agree on the principle of an independent commission, and by discussion here in parliament, the best kind of discussion, we will put our various views forward. Then by listening to the views put forward by others, we may come up with the kind of legislation that will not require basic changes every ten years.
I look forward to that being done, Mr. Chairman, because in the two previous decades in which I have been here, basic changes did have to be made. In the redistribution in the 1940's we took two bites at it. In the first place, although the government of the day, in the speech from the throne in 1943, said there would be redistribution in that session, it decided this was too contentious an issue to put before parliament during the war, so an amendment to the British North America Act was sought in order to postpone that redistribution, to postpone the contentious kind of debate it would have produced. It postponed most of the debate; but even the debate on the British North America Act amendment itself was a very contentious one and things were said which I think afterwards members perhaps thought were not to their credit and wished they were not recorded for all time.
Then when we did get at the matter in 1947 we had to make a basic change; we had to increase the size of the house from 245

Redistribution Commission seats to 262 for the 1949 election, so that the reductions in some of the provinces of the members they would have would not be too serious. Then when we got into the 1950's and came at the matter again, we had the problem of Saskatchewan losing too many seats because of the kind of adjustments in population that had taken place, so we had the formula that was written into the British North America Act at that time, which I think was proposed if not openly, certainly by understanding by the then minister of agriculture, Mr. Gardiner. At any rate, it was a pretty fundamental kind of change that we had to make, out of which we came up with 265 seats and these several variations in the general rule of representation among the provinces according to population.
If we are going to avoid having to make these basic changes every ten years, this job should be well done. I believe we all agree with the Leader of the Opposition that this is not something to rush. Let us look at the legislation carefully; let us study it carefully; let us come at it in the spirit that has been demonstrated thus far today by those who have spoken; and let us try to do as effective a job as we can, not for ourselves but for the Canadian people to whom parliament really belongs.
Now, Mr. Chairman, I would like to say a few words about some of the details. We have not seen them all yet; we have only those to which the Secretary of State has alluded in discussing the resolution, and those to which the Leader of the Opposition has alluded by comparing what might be with what his government proposed when the Conservatives were in office a year or two ago. We do have this question of whether there should be one commission or ten. Here I think we can discuss the matter in good faith. It is not a partisan issue, But I think it is good that we do have these two proposals before us. As a matter of fact we really have three proposals: the proposal for one commission; the proposal for four commissions, which the government is apparently not going to place before us; and the proposal for ten commissions, which is before us. I would like to suggest that we take a rather sympathetic look at the proposal for ten commissions. I appreciate the suggestion of the Leader of the Opposition that we have one for purposes of unity; but I think if each of us would consider the position in his own province he would realize that the chances of all the things that need to be considered receiving full consideration are best if there are people from that province doing the job for that particular province.
The Secretary of State indicated this afternoon that the government's plan would call

for ten commissions of four members each, one of whom would be the representation commissioner and the other three from the province concerned. I made reference to the independent commission that we have in the province of Manitoba for the purpose of provincial redistribution. I think the pattern we have in Manitoba is a good one and I dare to hope it is a pattern that might be followed. In our case the commission consists of the chief justice, the president of the University of Manitoba, and the chief electoral officer. If the government's plan goes through, the total commission for Manitoba would be those three and the representation commissioner. I think the representation commissioner sitting on all ten commissions would provide unity and consistency. On the other hand, having a commission for Manitoba consisting, as I hope might be the case, of Mr. Castonguay and the three persons I have already named from Manitoba, would produce a body which would not only be above any partisan consideration or reflection at all, it would not only be a board of efficiency-in Manitoba's case, one that has proven its capacity to do the job-but we would have three out of the four of that group being Manitoba people who would know the history, the geography and the people of Manitoba and would be able to take into consideration the points that need to be considered in order to draw the boundaries in the best interests, not of the members of parliament for Manitoba but in the best interests of the people of Manitoba themselves.
So I say, Mr. Chairman, let us look at these various proposals. I think the idea of ten commissions, one for each province, is a good one. I have already, by implication, joined in the tributes paid to Mr. Castonguay by the Secretary of State and the Leader of the Opposition. We think there was nothing inappropriate in the Secretary of State admitting that this is a name that has been considered, because this chief electoral officer, the son of a former chief electoral officer, both of whom have performed good service for this country, would certainly be an ideal person for this position. I agree that we should be given the names of those who will make up the commissions, or that we should know the device by which these names will be chosen. I was glad to hear the Secretary of State say that he does not think they should be chosen by order in council.
I would like to say a few words about another detail that the Leader of the Opposition discussed in his remarks. It is hardly a detail; it is pretty basic to the whole question. I refer to the matter of what tolerance there should be from a quota. The Leader of the Opposition told us that in the bill presented

by the previous government the proposal was that there be a tolerance of one third above or below the quota. When you work that out by mathematics, it means that the largest seat, in terms of population, could be twice the size of the smallest seat, in terms of population. When you realize that the former government's bill had-it was read to the committee this evening-escape hatches to go even further, you can see that a considerable disparity would be possible if there were that much tolerance.
The Leader of the Opposition threw out the figure of 20 per cent. Personally I think some such figure as that would be better. If you do your arithmetic again, you will realize that if you do allow a tolerance of only 20 per cent, the largest seat, in terms of population, can be only one and a half times the size of the population of the smallest seat. In all cases I am speaking about seats or constituencies inside a province. That leads to this whole question of the disparity or difference between rural and urban seats. I know the traditions about this and I readily recognize that this is something we do have to consider. Hon. members of course are aware of the fact that I represent one of those tightly knit urban constituencies. Though the population of Winnipeg North Centre is larger than the average across the country, the number of square miles of the constituency is very few. I say that just in case anyone thinks I am speaking from the standpoint of an urban member as against the two previous speakers, both of whom have spoken as rural members. That at least is on the record.
I think there are two aspects to this question, and we should try to keep them straight. On one hand there is the question of the weight that a Canadian elector's vote carries in parliament; on the other hand there is the question of a member being able to give service to his constituency. If you look only at the first of these considerations, namely the weight that a Canadian elector's vote carries in parliament, we should have representation by population. The numbers of people in all ridings should be equal. If they are not equal, then those who feel that there are twice as many of them in a constituency as in some other constituencies consider that they are not being adequately represented. But the other consideration is also a very real one. How can a member give service to his constituency if, in order to have the average number of electors in it or the average number of people, it has to be, in terms of square miles, literally an empire?
I suggest that we try and resolve this problem in two ways. On the one hand, let us admit some disparity by letting a figure such
28902-5-327J
Redistribution Commission as has been suggested be the rule, namely a 20 per cent tolerance up and down which would permit some constituencies to be one and a half times as large as others in terms of population. That is one way of admitting a certain amount of disparity. Another thing we can do-and now I speak as an urban member who cannot make any claim of this kind-is to recognize that members who serve large rural areas have problems of travel and communication that those of us in tightly packed urban areas do not have. I suppose in the light of what happened recently, any talk about extra expense money would not be popular, but should it not be in that area that we try to solve the problem of the member serving the rural area, rather than following a course which would result in urban people feeling that their votes are not as strong as those who live in the rural areas?
I have made my case as an urban member for something closer to representation by population, but I say quite frankly that a figure such as a 20 per cent tolerance up and down would, it seems to me, go a good way toward resolving the problem. However, I would propose that consideration be given also to extra travelling and communication expenses for those members in the large rural areas. I think, for example, to go to an extreme case, of the hon. member for Yukon and the hon. member for Northwest Territories. The distance they have to travel is much greater than the size of some provinces.
That may be just a detail, Mr. Chairman, as the Leader of the Opposition said, but it is a pretty important detail. We now have two suggestions coming from the lips of the Leader of the Opposition, either a 33J per cent tolerance, or a 20 per cent tolerance. Perhaps we can indulge in some collective bargaining here in the House of Commons and arrive at a figure between those two, but I am glad the pattern has been set for bringing these things out into the open and discussing them. I am also glad that the pattern has been set for objective, dispassionate and fair discussion of these matters so that we can seek to solve them and do what the Secretary of State hopes, namely to provide the kind of legislation which will not have to be changed every ten years as we go along. That is the story across the years so far. Basic changes in the legislation have been made every time to try to redress grievances and wrongs, or to try to avoid doing wrong to others. This time let us take our time and get the kind of proposals which will provide the greatest amount of fairness.
There was one other detail-we call these matters details, I suppose, to play them in low key, but they are pretty important-to

Redistribution Commission which the Secretary of State referred, and that concerned the case of Manitoba and Saskatchewan. He indicated that population changes in the last few years have been such that Manitoba now has a greater population by a few thousand than the province of Saskatchewan. At the moment there are 14 members from Manitoba and 17 from Saskatchewan. I am not going to set one of these provinces against the other by any means, but I do suggest that we must make sure that fairness is done between these two provinces. We also have to make sure that fairness is done to both of them in relation to the situation in the rest of Canada. I pride myself on being able to understand legislation and particularly mathematical formulae, but I find it hard to compute what would be the result of the present formula under the British North America Act which, when amended last time, gave Saskatchewan two more seats than otherwise it would have had. What effect that will have if we make no other changes to the B.N.A. Act this time I do not know; but if we make no other changes in the total representation and follow the rules set out in the B.N.A. Act we will still have 265 members. If that results, on the one hand, in Saskatchewan's having more members than Manitoba despite Manitoba's greater population, and on the other hand in both Saskatchewan and Manitoba losing members, despite their increased population, while British Columbia, Alberta, Ontario and Quebec increase their members, it is going to look as though an injustice has been done. I know it can be argued mathematically that they would be getting their proportionate numbers, but the loss of seats just would not do. We have the senatorial floor to protect us, but the senatorial floor is composed only of six members-

the parliament of Canada, as it has been known since 1867-we were set up with 181 seats. I have tried to ascertain what the population of Canada was in 1867; it is probably ascertainable but I have not got the figure for that year. The population of Canada, according to that census, was 14 million people. If we divide 14 million by the 265 seats provided then, it works out to a representation of about 58,000 Canadians per member. In other words, between 1867 and 1953, the year of the first election after the last redistribution, the number of people represented by each member increased from 20,000 to something like 58,000. Oh, no. Anyway that is a problem which could be solved easily by whoever is here after the next election.
We always enjoy discussions about redistribution and what the next election may produce. However, the main thing is for us to look at all the factors involved. Let us look at the various proposals which have been made with regard to an independent commission-whether there should be one or ten. Let us consider what the margin of tolerance should be. Let us consider the question of whether the report of an independent commission should be final or whether provision should be made for review. Let us consider, also, the question of how many members there should be in order to be fair to the country as a whole.
There is one thing on which we seem to be agreed. We have agreed that no longer should the drawing of constituency boundaries be done by a parliamentary committee but that it should be carried out by an independent commission. To have reached agreement in that regard, is good. Now let us have the kind of debate we have had thus far; let us sort out the various proposals and come up with a plan which will not have to be changed. Then let us get on with the job.
I see you are on the edge of your chair, Mr. Chairman. I do not intend to detain the committee much longer. Even though we must give this matter the thorough study it deserves I hope we can deal with it with reasonable expedition. I would say that the Secretary of State set a reasonable goal when he suggested that this measure should be got through before Christmas so that the commission could be set up and a start made. We never know when an election could happen in this country. We have learned that from experience. Let us ensure as far as we can that the next election will be based on a redistribution according to the 1961 census. The 1945 parliamentary elections were held on a redistribution based on the 1931 census which was completely outdated. In 1963 we had an election on a redistribution based on the 1951 census and that, too, was outdated. Let us not have another election in the 'sixties based on the 1951 census. Let us have it on the basis of the 1961 census. I think that by proper expedition we can achieve that object.
I am glad the Secretary of State has made it clear that when we have the bills before us the details can be changed without there being any question of want of confidence in the government. Let us discuss this matter in a spirit of collective bargaining and come up with decisions which will stand the test of time. Let us turn the debate on redistribution

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, we welcome the opportunity presented to us at this time to discuss some of the matters which are of such vital interest and concern to us, as they relate to our electoral system.
As in many other fields of national concern it seems we have been very slow to effect the changes which are needed so as to eliminate some of the inadequacies apparent in our electoral system in Canada. From time to time certain changes have been made, but it would appear they have been made, not on the basis of principle but on the basis of expediency and political considerations. It would seem to me the time has come-and this view has been expressed by previous speakers-when we should take a good look at the whole situation and endeavour to make those changes which will be to the advantage not only of parliamentarians but of Canadians as a whole.
For these reasons, we welcome the introduction of these particular measures. We believe they will have a beneficial effect upon our parliamentary system. On a number of occasions various aspects of this question have been debated in the house, but unfortunately they were discussed at times when there was little possibility of the house reaching any decisions with regard to them. Now that these matters have been presented to us for consideration we trust that the fullest consideration will be given to every consideration put forward. We hope that those suggestions which are worth while will be incorporated in the measures and that those which are not important will be sifted out and cast aside.
We are, of course, aware of the fact that this problem has been occupying the attention not only of those who sit in this house but of many other agencies across the country. For instance, our attention was directed some time ago to certain recommendations of the federation of mayors and municipalities. Even though we might not be able to support all those recommendations, the federation has brought to our attention one of the basic problems which has been referred to tonight, the achievement of fair representation according to population. I think we all agree these are problems that must not only be recognized but met. I believe the Secretary of State characterized this matter as one of the most important issues that could occupy our attention at this time, and with that I agree.
The problem has perhaps been caused by the wholesale shifting in population from area to area which has seen a tremendous concentration of population in certain sections and at the same time has resulted, of course,


in a diminishing of population in other sections, notably the rural areas. The matter of geographical areas has also been referred to tonight. In my view this is a very important consideration, because of the fact that a member of parliament can only cover adequately a certain area and fulfil his responsibility to a certain number of people.
Another important factor is the availability of the member to his constituents. Not only must he be able to get around and see them at certain times or so many times in the course of a year, but those who have problems must be able to get to their member and we recognize that he must be accessible to them at such times. We think also of the industrial and social considerations that enter into the whole problem and the serious imbalance that now exists in representation. All these problems have been covered in the discussion today. I believe they are very serious considerations and we must give them our attention.
On October 12, 1962 the hon. member for Port Arthur brought in a private member's bill regarding redistribution. He pointed out a number of these problems, made certain deductions and arrived at certain conclusions. On that occasion as well as others we have had the opportunity to face up to some of the problems that confront us.
I suppose a completely satisfactory and equitable solution will not be possible in every instance, but we must make a sincere and concerted effort to resolve as many problems as we possibly can so that, as has been pointed out tonight, it will not be necessary within a very short time to make any fundamental or basic changes in the legislation. The measures that are before us are designed to solve some of the problems in order to make our electoral system conform more to present day requirements.
Words of commendation have been uttered with regard to the chief electoral officer for the work he has done during past years. We in this group would like to concur in those words of appreciation and commendation, because we believe he has fulfilled in a wonderful way the responsibilities that have devolved upon him in that office. The suggestions we have before us tonight are perhaps based to a considerable degree upon recommendations and suggestions he has made following his extensive study of the various problems. The fact that he has had the opportunity of discussing these problems in other countries, and looking at their problems and the way in which they have endeavoured to solve them, has no doubt had a real influence upon his own thinking in this regard. I am sure we are indebted to the chief electoral officer for what he has done in respect of these matters.

If I may deal with some of the issues that have been raised tonight, the fact that we are being asked to appoint a representation commissioner and subsequently a commission indicates a recognition that certain things should be above partisan politics, and surely this is one area in which this must be true. As has been indicated, no doubt in the past some decisions have been based upon political considerations rather than upon a sincere endeavour to resolve the problems and work out the boundary lines between constituencies on an equitable basis. But we believe that by appointing an independent commission we will go far toward removing that rather obnoxious element from redistribution.
The question of the necessity of a full time representation commissioner has been raised. Perhaps it has not been raised in the debate thus far, but it certainly has in various private discussions that have been held. We have been wondering whether it is absolutely necessary that such a commissioner be appointed. We have already paid tribute to the work that has been done by the chief electoral officer and it might be in order to suggest that we should consider whether the duties of the representation commissioner could not be combined with those of the chief electoral officer, and his staff possibly expanded. It appears that there could be a duplication of activities between the chief electoral officer and the representation commissioner and perhaps this could be avoided by adding to the staff of the chief electoral officer and allowing him to discharge the responsibilities of the two offices. I am not making a definite recommendation but simply suggesting this as something that could be given consideration.
Another question raised tonight concerns the advisability of having ten commissions rather than having one, or four, as previously suggested. I must admit that formerly I have viewed the idea of possibly four commissions as being practical and desirable, but in the way that the suggestion of ten commissions has been put before us I can definitely see that there are advantages. For one thing, it will save time and I believe this is a very important consideration. We heard this afternoon that the appointment of one commission would result in the postponement until possibly 1968 of any election that could be held based upon the new redistribution. Even if four commissions were appointed I suppose it would take a considerable length of time. However, ten commissions should be able to proceed with their task with dispatch and complete their work in a much shorter period of time.
Redistribution Commission I believe the Secretary of State pointed out that having ten commissions would not involve any substantial additional expenditure because in all probability the commissioners would be paid on a per diem basis, but as they would be called on to serve for a shorter period of time it would simply mean that the cost would be spread over a greater number of people. The fact that the commissioners will in all probability be chosen from their respective provinces is also an important consideration. If one commission were appointed with members from all parts of the country from coast to coast, the commissioners would have to spend much more time acquainting themselves with the provincial and local area situations; but by having one commission for each province the commissioners will be more aware of the problems in their own provinces. Therefore, speaking personally and also, I think, for our group, I can say that we look with favour upon the proposal to have ten commissions, rather than one or four as previously suggested.
We appreciate the fact that parliamentary responsibility is being maintained, even although the independent commission is doing the work of redrawing the boundary lines. On the other occasion to which I referred, when the hon. member for Port Arthur was speaking on this matter, he pressed the idea of a completely independent board. I feel that there should be some responsibility to parliament in this respect so far as these commissions are concerned. It would seem to me to be a repudiation of responsibility were we to turn this work over completely to an independent commission, without any review of it here in this house. We trust that when any measure is brought before us adequate provision will be made for a thorough analysis and study of the recommendations, and every opportunity given to voice opinions in this particular respect.
Now, Mr. Chairman, the various matters have been covered very thoroughly today. The speakers have gone into a great deal of history, given historical reviews and quoted from speakers of bygone days. I do not propose to do that, because there has been sufficient placed on the record in regard to these matters.
However, I should like to refer to the suggestion made by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre to the effect that it would not be such a bad idea if we were to increase the membership of this house rather than reduce the representation of some provinces. By the way, in passing, I should like to say that I hope when the Secretary of State referred to the fact that British Columbia was under-represented at the present time he meant it as far as numbers were concerned,
5138	HOUSE OF
Redistribution Commission and not as far as quality was concerned. As to the increase in membership of this house, I do not know whether or not that would be desirable. We have 265 members here, and there are 102 members in the other place. We have ten provincial legislatures with varying numbers. We have our municipal governments; and it would almost seem to me that Canada is pretty well governed so far as numbers and so far as agencies are concerned. I do not know, therefore, if the suggestion should be taken too seriously. Certainly, consideration should be given to it, but I think possibly we should look at it from the other point of view and discover whether or not it would be in the best interest of the nation to increase the membership in this parliament.
With these observations, Mr. Chairman, I will leave this matter. No doubt other members of this group will be participating in the debate. They certainly will when we come to debate the various items in the bill that will be presented after this resolution.

Mr. Chairman, I see that the young backbenchers of the Liberal party have yet not renounced their little game of interrupting. I know that nothing hurts like the truth, but never mind. It is a good thing from time to time to spread truth around, and we do not feel shy about it.
Mr. Chairman, I would absolutely oppose any increase in the number of members if they were all like the hon. member for Mercier (Mr. Boulanger) who never takes the floor but spends his time interrupting.
On the other hand, if an increase in the number of members did not impede the business of the house, but would prevent us from wasting our time as we are doing now, I would be in favour of such an increase.
In fact, at present, with 265 members, we are not even able to pass the necessary legislation within the allotted time. That is one of the reasons why I am against an increase in the size of the house.
It is true, as the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) pointed out, that in 1867, each member represented 20,000 people, while in 1951, there was one member for 58,000 Canadians. Under the present bill, one member would represent 70,000 people.
Mr. Chairman, let us not forget that nowadays means of transportation and communication are much quicker than they were in days gone by.
In fact, it is much easier nowadays than in 1867, 1925 or even 1930 for the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre to go in his riding and meet his voters during a week end.
Mr. Chairman, I am of the opinion that if a member is elected for a certain number of voters, the number of problems to be settled will increase, because it has been noted that most of the problems to be solved by hon. members for their voters come from vexatious interference from government officials. It is not that government officials are wicked. No. But as I said before, because of the great number of complicated acts that they must apply, they are quite difficult to deal with.

Most of the problems that members of this house have to deal with, on behalf of their constituents, result from government and bureaucratic red tape concerning the administration of very complicated legislation such as, for instance, the Unemployment Insurance Act and, more especially, the Income Tax Act.
Indeed, Mr. Chairman, numerous problems are raised by income tax officials who take it upon themselves to cut down, without making any investigation and in an arbitrary and discriminatory fashion, charitable donations receipts to be used for income tax deductions. Consequently, if we are to represent 70,000 voters instead of 20,000, that, for us, will mean more cases to deal with. And I say again that such a situation is due to the fact that government officials have to apply vexatious laws.
If, instead of increasing the number of members, we were given more help to settle those matters, I think the problem would be solved. As a matter of fact, I would suggest that the number of senators be reduced instead.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR OFFICE OF REPRESENTATION COMMISSIONER AND READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION
speechtext:
I notice that the hon. member for Mercier is leaving the house; he realizes that his next job is disappearing.
Mr. Chairman, I would like to deal with another problem tonight: that of the independent commission that will look after this redistribution.
In fact, we are in favour of the setting up of an independent commission that would look after the redistribution and we support that plan. However, that commission should be really independent. But who would appoint the commissioners? Would it be only the Secretary of State (Mr. Pickersgill) who would appoint some friends of the government?
Before agreeing to the principle of an independent commission, we must decide that it will be really independent and that its members will be chosen by the five political parties in the house. Then we will be sure that commission will be truly independent.
We are told: The returning officers in the various ridings must be independent. But they are appointed by the party in power about every ten years or even more often. Sure, they are independent, but there is nothing to prevent them from leaning on one side more than on the other, and they will tend to lean towards the party that appointed them rather than towards the others.
The chief returning officer of an electoral district, even if he is supposed to be independent, is still appointed by the party in office and often, since the law gives him
Redistribution Commission some leeway, he will use it to favour the party that appointed him rather than the others.
I feel it is essential that the commissioners be appointed by the five political parties represented in this house.
I should now like to deal with the most important problem to which this resolution will give rise, and that is: how many ridings will there be? What provinces are going to lose some and what provinces are going to gain some?
A study has been made, and I have here a few figures showing that Canada has a population of 18,238,247. If you leave out the ten ridings in New Brunswick, which must remain unchanged, the four ridings in Prince Edward Island, the one in Yukon and the other in the Northwest Territories, which make 16, there is left a total of 249 ridings. The population of those 16 counties being 740,191, there are 17,498,056 inhabitants left in the other ridings, or an average of 70,842 people for each of the 249 remaining ridings.
According to the predictions I have here, the number of ridings should be reduced from 265 to 264; the province of Quebec would have 74 seats instead of 75, other provinces would lose seats, the number of seats in Ontario would increase from 85 to 88, other provinces would gain seats: British Columbia would gain 1, Alberta 2, and Saskatchewan would lose 4.

Mr. Chairman, in the province of Quebec, one of the main arguments put forward by the separatists is the following: "As things are going now, they say, before the year two thousand, instead of having 75 representatives in Ottawa out of 265, this province will only have half of this number and this means that French Canadians will

Redistribution Commission be represented in this house not by 34 or 35 per cent of the members, but only by 18, 15 or even 12 per cent.
It must be recognized, however, that the percentage of French Canadians will not decrease in the province of Quebec, but we will lose some representatives in the House of Commons. This is one of the most important arguments set forth by the protagonists of separatism.
Mr. Chairman, I have a suggestion to make to the Secretary of State which, I think, he should take into consideration. It is admitted that for New Brunswick, the number of members should not be less than ten; for Prince Edward Island, it should not be less than four.
I submit then, keeping the number of 265 members for Canada, that the province of Quebec should never have less than 75 members.
This would eliminate one of the main arguments of the protagonists of the separatist doctrine in the province of Quebec. It would also guarantee to French Canadians who view this problem with alarm that they will always have adequate representation in the House of Commons, even if their ratio decreases compared to Canada as a whole.
Following immigration, our group represents a lesser percentage of the over-all population because immigrants are more easily assimilated by English speaking Canada than by French speaking Canada.
We have nothing against that. It is not the fault of English Canadians if immigrants join their ranks rather than ours. It is our fault and we must take the blame when we deserve it.
However, I feel that we must ensure that French Canadians are adequately represented in the House of Commons. I would, therefore, suggest that the province of Quebec should never have less than 75 members out of a total of 265 or similar representation if there are more or less than 265 members in the house.
I know that Quebec will also elect English speaking members as is the case at present for the Minister of Industry and Defence Production-

-whose competence honours his province. Forgive me, I meant the minister of peacetime defence production whose competence is the pride of Quebec. We are glad that the English speaking citizens of Quebec have elected such a representative. We feel that English Canadians who live in our province must also be represented in the house. As I say, we are glad to see that

But we feel that-

speechtext:
The hon. member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm thinks only in terms of patronage which, as I know, is far from being the case for the other member I am speaking of.
Mr. Chairman, it is true that some English speaking members from the province of Quebec will come to Ottawa. We do not object to that. But in the province of Quebec, the percentage of French Canadians has not come down. It holds up regularly. I think that if we accept as an absolute policy that the percentage of members coming from the province of Quebec to Ottawa will always remain unchanged, we will put an end to one of the greatest fears of the French Canadians in the province of Quebec and even throughout the country.
I think that at this time, when there is so much talk about biculturalism and bilingualism-as far as I am concerned, I see biculturalism as a system allowing two cultures to develop-if we really wish to have biculturalism, we should take an opportunity such as this to put into the statutes of Canada a provision to the effect that the French Canadians will always be adequately represented in the House of Commons at Ottawa.
If 35 or 40 years from now we should make up only 10 per cent of the population and have by then only 10 per cent of the members in the House of Commons we would then have to confess that we failed to provide today for future generations. I believe that we should see to it now that the French Canadians will forever be present in sufficient numbers in this house.
We make this suggestion to the Secretary of State in the hope that he will consider it earnestly in the drafting of the bill.
If I may, I would like to mention a fact which shows that this suggestion has already been carried out in the province of Quebec, where we maintain that the English Canadian minorities receive very fair treatment. I do not remember in what year the Quebec legislature determined the number of counties, but they determined that number so as to safeguard the English Canadian

minorities' rights, and more particularly so in the eastern townships, where they gave those counties the assurance that they would continue to exist even if there were disproportion as far as the number of their electors is concerned. That is the reason why we have those small counties like Brome-Missis-quoi, Compton, Shefford and Stanstead in the provincial field. The existence of those counties was respected by the provincial government. Why? When the Quebec legislature ordered a redistribution, it wanted to guarantee an adequate representation of English minorities in the province, by leaving them some counties which, today, are represented only by a minimum of voters.
In my opinion, Mr. Chairman, the same thing can be done at the federal level, since we in the province of Quebec have been able to guarantee to English Canadians an adequate representation at the provincial legislative assembly. I am of the opinion that the federal government ought to adopt the same policy towards the French Canadian minority in the province of Quebec and guarantee the existence of a certain number of ridings in order to enable French Canadians to claim their rights in the house at any time in the future.
That would set a tremendous example for future generations, as far as the right of the French Canadian nation to have an adequate representation in parliament is concerned.
Moreover, it is already done for some provinces. For instance, Prince Edward Island, with a population of 104,629 has four guaranteed ridings, which gives an average of
26,000	people per riding, when the other ridings in Canada have an average of 70,842 people, according to the last census. We uphold this principle and what applies to Prince Edward Island should also apply to the province of Quebec.
